intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honor all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 1234969563: an empty nest with a terrible memory for faces, filling batteries. Here's how that became a night in the gutter.

rolls.value: an empty nest with a terrible memory for faces
rolls.became: A nest in the gutter of a family house. Its chicks fledged and flew south in September, and it can't remember what they looked like. That one flaw explains the whole game: it can't tell a chirping smoke alarm from a hungry chick, or a passing bird from its own kid.
The nest fills batteries with charge, a few sparks at a time, the way it would warm a clutch.

Low-battery devices really do chirp, and smoke alarms really do chirp more at three in the morning, because cold makes a battery sag. To a nest that can't remember faces, the house below is full of hungry chicks. Full batteries are the only thing that shuts them up.

rolls.value: trace a rune to cast it
rolls.became: Runes are all straight strokes because they were made for carving into wood, and a nest is nothing but wood. Trace the rune over the nest and twig rubs on twig until the static fills the cell in the bowl. Kenaz the torch first, then Sowilo, Thurisaz and Dagaz, each worth more sparks.
Nothing goes past the hundreds: 330 mouths to feed across the house, a feeder that holds 999 seeds (the squirrels get the rest), and a flock of up to 60 birds.

A nest is a machine for feeding mouths. Its own mouths have gone, so it feeds whatever chirps: the TV remote, the kitchen clock, the cat's laser pointer, two smoke alarms, the camping lantern, the car.

Every chirp only lasts until dawn, shown as the ring running out round its bubble. Miss it and Dad changes the battery himself, from a packet. The nest takes this personally. Lullaby makes the chirps wait longer.

Priya, eight, who lives in the house. She caught a bird sitting on the smoke alarm one night, and since then she has kept a chart: every quiet night, seed in the feeder. That seed is the game's money.

Night migrants rest by day on their way south. The nest greets each one as its own kid home early, gets its name wrong, and puts it to work: brooding (warming a cold battery really does bring some charge back), packing, or carrying batteries down the drainpipe.

rolls.value: craft: trade many of A for one B
rolls.became: A 9-volt really is six tiny cells in a box, so the nest has decided every big battery is small ones packed together: six AA for a 9-volt, four 9-volts for a lantern battery, five lanterns for a car battery. Nobody has corrected it.

rolls.value: demand or a picky critic to please
rolls.became: The house is the demand. Each device asks for its own size, and each room only opens once the one before it has been fed enough times: living room, hallway, garage, driveway.

rolls.value: one last purchase that costs everything
rolls.became: The Last Feast: every seed in the feeder and every battery in the bowl.

Birds really do feast before they migrate, until they're heavy enough to fly a long way. Heavy enough to carry a nest by the ribbon handles it wove on for no reason. The batteries go on Priya's windowsill so the house stays quiet all winter, and the nest goes south with a flock it never once recognised.
Everything is a lump of clay: soft shadows, a shine up and to the left, wobbly edges. The car and the cat are icons squashed into clay; the nest, the birds and Priya are made by hand.
Six colours of an autumn night: plum dark, indigo and slate clay, steel twigs, and mint for anything with charge in it.
A handheld console's lullaby in A harmonic minor, that raised seventh giving it a little night-time mystery. Voices join as rooms open, and the sound effects stay on the same scale.
A hushed narrator who takes the nest's mistakes completely seriously, and keeps the real facts straight.
No calendar nod: just late autumn and a first frost.

outro: Nobody has told the nest where it's going. It has a postcard of a beach, and a feeling.
